explain.say: Electrons do not buzz around the nucleus just anywhere. They live in layers called shells, a bit like the layers of an onion. Look at the board. This is a sodium atom, and you have 11 electrons to fit in.

explain.say: Into a new third shell! See it glowing on the outside? You write sodium as 2, 8, 1. That lonely outer electron is easy to lose, which is why sodium reacts so fiercely with water. Can you work out oxygen, with 8 electrons?

explain.say: It is 2, 6! Brilliant, you are getting good at this. Now look at the groups: atoms with the same number of outer electrons behave alike, which is how the periodic table is arranged. Wow: neon and argon have full outer shells and hardly react, so argon is used to fill light bulbs.

faq.a: Outer electrons are the ones in the outermost shell. They decide how an atom reacts, because they are the ones that are lost, gained or shared.

faq.q: How many electrons fit in each shell?
faq.a: For the first 20 elements, the first shell holds 2 electrons and the next two shells hold 8 each. Shells fill from the inside out.

faq.q: How do you write an electron configuration?
faq.a: Count the electrons, which equal the atomic number, then fill the shells: 2 first, then 8, then 8. Sodium, with 11 electrons, is 2, 8, 1.
asks: How do I work out the electronic structure?

faq.a: Sodium has one electron alone in its outer shell. It loses that electron very easily, so it reacts quickly, even fizzing on water.
asks: Why does sodium react with water?

faq.q: How does the electron arrangement link to the periodic table?
faq.a: The number of outer electrons gives the group, and the number of shells gives the period. Sodium, 2, 8, 1, is in group 1 and period 3.
asks: What do shells tell you about group and period?

facts: For the first 20 elements, the first shell holds up to 2 electrons and the second and third shells hold up to 8.
